author: val
body: SAKAMOTO'S METHOD, and the table is his. `t` corrects each month for the lengths of the ones before it; the year is stepped back for January and February so that a leap day falls at the END of the adjusted year and the three division terms count leap years without a special case. It answers 0 for Sunday.

body: THE NTH WEEKDAY, AND "LAST" IS N = 0. Every summer time rule in the table is phrased as one of these two and nothing else, so these two are the whole of what the rules need to ask of a calendar.

author: val
body: THE SOUTHERN INTERVAL WRAPS THE YEAR END, and that is the whole reason this is not one comparison. Above the equator summer time starts in spring and ends in autumn, so its interval sits inside the year and `start <= now < end` is right. Below it, summer time starts in October and ends in April: the interval crosses the new year, `start` is GREATER than `end`, and the same test answers backwards for exactly the people who live there.

body: Every rule in the table moves the clock by exactly one hour. Lord Howe Island moves by thirty minutes and is not in the table; if it ever is, this answers the rule rather than the constant.

author: val
body: MIDNIGHT IS 12 AM AND NOON IS 12 PM, which is the one place a twelve hour clock is not arithmetic. Hour 0 prints as 12 and hour 12 prints as 12, and the two differ only in the suffix.
